tone_statements.citation: Sarmah, Priyankoo. 2009. Tone systems of Dimasa and Rabha: a phonetic and phonological study. PhD dissertation, University of Florida. 157 pp.
tone_statements.quote: As far as the number of tones is concerned, this study concludes that in both Dimasa and Rabha, there are three phonological tones or tonemes. … Depending on the shape of the pitch contour, it is assessed that Dimasa and Rabha have a rising (R), falling (F) and a mid-level (M) tone. … in both Dimasa and Rabha underived words, only one lexical tone is underlyingly specified and that lexical tone is associated with the rightmost syllable of word. Any syllable that is devoid of an underlying lexical tone is assigned an unmarked mid-level tone …
tone_statements.locator: ch. 7 Conclusion, 'Tone Inventories' p. 136 and 'General Tone Assignment Pattern' p. 140

tone_statements.citation: Hammarström, Harald. 2009. Review of U. V. Joseph, Rabha (Languages of the Greater Himalayan Region 1; Leiden: Brill, 2007). Himalayan Linguistics Review 9: 1-3. (eScholarship item 2k1868js; Crossref lists it under Himalayan Linguistics with DOI 10.5070/H91224530 and year 2014.)
tone_statements.quote: The phonology section is high in detail, and has minimal pairs for the 18 consonants, 6 vowels, plus a two-way tonal contrast (see below). ... One especially exciting section in this chapter is that on tonogenesis, for Bodo and Rabha have phonemic tone, while Garo arguably does not. Garo has a glottal stop, shown by the author to be in perfect correlation with Bodo and Rabha tone, and in addition, Bodo has replaced a final -k in Rabha and Garo with tone (pp. 496-509).
tone_statements.locator: review p. 1 (paragraph on the phonology section) and p. 2 (paragraph on the correlative analysis chapter); Himalayan Linguistics Review 9 (2009)
tone_statements.summary: Per the reviewer, Joseph 2007 analyses Rabha with a two-way (phonemic) tonal contrast supported by minimal pairs, and derives Bodo/Rabha tone historically in correlation with the Garo glottal stop (tonogenesis, pp. 496-509 of the grammar). Nothing on stress or tone-bearing unit in the review.

tone_statements.citation: Central Institute of Indian Languages. n.d. Rabha: Structure of language (Language Information Service - India web description; companion page 'Rabha History'). Mysore: CIIL, lisindia.ciil.org.
tone_statements.quote: Rabha does not have phonemic stress, length and nasalization. But it has the phonemic tone. For example high / rising mid / level low / falling / tshó / 'to burn' / tshō / 'mosquito' / sho`/ 'to spite' … 2.2.7.3 Tone: Tone is not prominent in most of the Rabha dialects except Kocha. Due to syllabic stress, the tone shift has become the common feature in Rongdani and Maitori dialects. However three tones are marked in Rabha language.e.g. (i) high(raising) (ii) mid (neutral) (ii)low(falling) / tshó / 'to burn' / tshŌ / 'mosquito' / tshÒ / 'to spite'
tone_statements.summary: Three phonemic tones: high (rising), mid (level), low (falling), shown on monosyllables; tone called prominent only in the Kocha dialect; stress called non-phonemic though stress pairs are listed.

sources.citation: Sarmah, Priyankoo. 2009. Tone systems of Dimasa and Rabha: a phonetic and phonological study. PhD dissertation, University of Florida. 157 pp.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Nothing on Rabha word stress. Rabha has three tones (H, M, L); in disyllables the initial syllable carries a default mid tone and the single lexical tone is realised on the rightmost syllable (pp. 89, 139-140); in suffixed words only the rightmost (suffix) tone survives.

tone.quote: As far as the number of tones is concerned, this study concludes that in both Dimasa and Rabha, there are three phonological tones or tonemes. … Depending on the shape of the pitch contour, it is assessed that Dimasa and Rabha have a rising (R), falling (F) and a mid-level (M) tone. … in both Dimasa and Rabha underived words, only one lexical tone is underlyingly specified and that lexical tone is associated with the rightmost syllable of word. Any syllable that is devoid of an underlying lexical tone is assigned an unmarked mid-level tone …
tone.locator: ch. 7 Conclusion, 'Tone Inventories' p. 136 and 'General Tone Assignment Pattern' p. 140
tone.says: Three tones, rising, falling and mid-level (acoustic study); one lexical tone per word on its final syllable, other syllables default mid; a suffix keeps its tone and the stem goes mid.

sources.note: 4.3 Tone (p. 205): two tones, high and low, 'each syllable is characterized phonologically by a distinct tone'. No stress section. Ch. 2 summarises Joseph 2007's phonology (segments, clusters, tone, syllable) with no mention of stress.

sources.citation: Koch, Jibeswar. 2014. Rabha dialects: a linguistic study. PhD thesis, Gauhati University. (Shodhganga 10603/116528; ch. II 'The Rabha language and its linguistic variations' pp. 8-74 read)
sources.note: 2.1.4 Tones (pp. 17-18): two tones; Maitori and Rongdani 'fairly identical, in both tone and accentuation'. No rule for stress placement.

sources.citation: Joseph, U. V. & Robbins Burling. 2006. The Comparative Phonology of the Boro-Garo Languages. Mysore: Central Institute of Indian Languages.
sources.note: 'Rabha Tones' pp. 25-26: two tones (high: short, glottalised in monosyllables; low); high tone on 1st syllable spreads right; in uninflected disyllables only high-high, neutral-high, neutral-low patterns occur. No statement about stress in Rabha (stress is mentioned only as an English analogy for Tiwa falling tone, pp. 9-11).

sources.citation: Basumatary, Phukan Chandra. 2004. A study in cultural and linguistic affinities of the Boros and the Rabhas of Assam. PhD thesis, Gauhati University. (Shodhganga 10603/66580; ch. 3 Phonology pp. 79-96 read)
sources.note: 3.2 Tones (pp. 90-91): high vs unmarked low; 'usually only one tone marking is allowed either in mono-syllabic or poly-syllabic word'. No stress statement.

sources.citation: Joseph, U. V. & Robbins Burling. 2001. Tone correspondences among the Bodo languages. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 24(2): 41-55.
sources.note: Rabha section p. 50: high vs low tone, pitch the salient cue, tones spread rightward, glottal stop only word-/utterance-final. Nothing on stress; authors say they do not know whether Rabha tones can attach to different syllable positions as in Tiwa (p. 51).

sources.citation: Hildebrandt, Kristine A. 2011. Review of "Languages of the Greater Himalayan Region, vol. 1: Rabha" [U. V. Joseph, Brill 2007]. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 34(1).
sources.note: Reviewer refers to a high tone (acute-marked, with rightward spread) and a low tone in Joseph's 2007 description; tone interacts with vowel length and glottalization; no count or analysis given here.

tone.quote: First: tone, where an acoustic profile (even if rudimentary) would greatly help in illustrating the system, as it is interwoven with vowel qualities like length and glottalization. Aside from a brief mention of rightward spread of the high tone, there is very little discussion of the domain of tone or sandhi phenomena. The author acknowledges (p. 56) that more work is needed, and admittedly tone is dealt with more carefully in Chapter 7. … They are /oi, ai, ao, au, ui, eo, eu, iu/ and /ɨi/ (all with low tone), and /ái, áo/ and /ói/ (with high tone).
tone.locator: p. 140, comments on Chapter 2 (Sound Level Analysis)

sources.citation: Burling, Robbins. [1995-2005]. Notes on Rabha field work and word lists. Unpublished field notes, 42 pp. (typed report 'Rabha.' on scan pp. 2-3, handwritten word lists and vowel notes pp. 4-42). Denton, TX: University of North Texas Digital Library, CoRSAL collection, local no. rah_acq2022_02, ark:/67531/metadc2062338.
sources.note: After the initials/finals/vowel inventory Burling writes that he 'got no hint of tones' - a first-contact impression that his own later work reversed (Joseph & Burling 2001, 2006: two tones, in the works listed here). Historically useful as the pre-2001 baseline; not a valid description of the tone system.

tone.quote: Vowels appear to be of the familiar sort: ... The hight variation in open and closed syllables seems a bit more pronounced than in some languages, but I do not think that it implies any sort of contrast. I got no hint of tones and would be very surprised if there are any. tone contrasts. There is some assimilation across syllable boundaries which I certainly did not get to the botom of.
tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.summary: States no tone contrast was heard (preliminary fieldwork impression, six sessions, elicitation through Garo); gives initials ph th kh ch / p t k / b d g j / m n / r l w s z h, finals p t k m n ng r, six vowels incl. high back unrounded, diphthongs ai au oi; nothing on stress. Superseded by the author's published two-tone analysis (Joseph & Burling 2001: 41-55; 2006: 25-26).
